title: Well proclaimed
hook: a teaching well proclaimed survives its teacher's death
tomorrow: The marks of a great man

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sariputta's checked confidence. Your line: here is why I trust it. Today news arrives of a teacher's death, and a worry about what comes next.

A young novice named Cunda has spent the rainy season near the town of Pava, and he has watched something unravel there. A well-known teacher of the time, Nigantha Nataputta, has died, and his followers have split into camps, each telling the other it has the teaching wrong. When the rains end, Cunda walks to Samagama, where Ananda is staying, and tells him everything. Ananda doesn't pass the story along. He thinks of his own community and says: friend Cunda, this is worth bringing to the Blessed One. Let's go and tell him.
screen: `A NOVICE AT PAVA.` → `A COMMUNITY SPLITS.` → `ANANDA: TAKE THIS TO THE TEACHER.`

segments.voice: Nigantha Nataputta is the teacher the Jain tradition honors as Mahavira, and Jains tell of his passing in their own texts and their own way. The Pasadika Sutta, the pleasing discourse, uses the news only as a starting point and turns to the Buddha's own followers. What keeps a teaching alive after its teacher dies? The Buddha's answer has two parts. First, it has to be well proclaimed: clearly taught, complete, its meaning made plain, so students aren't left guessing. Second, the students have to keep it that way. So he gives them a job. Come together, all of you, and recite what I have taught, comparing meaning with meaning and wording with wording, so this holy life may last long, for the welfare of many. And if a fellow student recites a teaching and the wording or the meaning seems off, don't applaud and don't scorn. Ask, gently: friend, which fits better, this wording or that? This meaning or that? Keep asking until it's clear. It's the habit of the four great references from a couple of weeks ago, now practiced together, out loud, kindly. And it's why the discourses still exist. For centuries they weren't written down at all. People carried them by sitting together, reciting, checking each other, and keeping the words clear. A teaching well proclaimed, held by students who keep proclaiming it well.
screen: `NEWS OF A TEACHER'S PASSING.` · `TAUGHT CLEARLY, AND COMPLETE.` · `RECITE IT TOGETHER.` · `FRIEND, WHICH FITS BETTER?` · then, large: `WELL PROCLAIMED.`

segments.voice: Choose one teaching you care about, from this path or anywhere, and say it to yourself in one clear sentence. Ask the sutta's gentle question, is this the right wording, the right meaning, then adjust it and say it again. Let it rest clear in the background as you sit with the breath.
Well proclaimed. In DN 29 the Buddha says a clearly taught teaching, kept clear by students reciting together, survives its teacher. Today's word.
Your line: ask gently, which fits better. A clear teaching, kept clear by friends. Day five hundred sixty-three, done.

screen: `DAY 563 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE MARKS OF A GREAT MAN.`

howItsDone: Buddhist monastics in many traditions still memorize and chant the discourses together, and the great councils of the tradition, from the first after the Buddha's death to modern ones, were recitations checked in common.

fork.setup: you're Ananda. a novice brings news that a famous teacher has died and his followers are quarreling. what do you do?
options: spread the news around the monastery.
take it to the Buddha, thinking of your own community's future.
ignore it: it's not your concern.
fork.reveal: Ananda says it's worth bringing to the Blessed One, and the Buddha teaches how a teaching stays whole: recite it together.

original.note: Pali svakkhata: well proclaimed. the first word of the classic praise of the Dhamma.

trapdoor: what you thought: teachings survive because they're written down.
what it means: in DN 29 they survive by being taught clearly and recited together, checked kindly.
what a scholar hears: DN 29 and DN 33 both open with the Nigantha schism at Pava and urge communal recitation (sangayana), the same word later used for the Buddhist councils.
recall: a standard to check a teaching against

chat.says: How did the Buddha's teachings last so long without being written down?
options: Students recited together, checking wording and meaning, and corrected gently.
One senior monk memorized it all and recited it alone every year.
Each town kept its own version, and nobody ever compared them.
chat.meaning: In DN 29 the Buddha asks students to recite together, meaning with meaning and wording with wording, and to ask gently which fits better.

notes: DN 29 paraphrased. Confirm: Cunda the novice brings the news to Ananda at Samagama; the instruction to recite together comparing meaning and phrasing; the gentle correction procedure.
Nigantha Nataputta is identified with Mahavira; the script defers to Jain accounts and passes no judgment. Keepers should confirm this is fair and brief.
svakkhata in the 'original' game: check Devanagari spelling (स्वाक्खात) and pronunciation.
'Not written down for centuries': the Pali canon is traditionally said to have been written in Sri Lanka in the first century BCE; general statement.
